implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy's unit of work is the parent's mapper: declare lines = relationship("OrderLine", cascade="all, delete-orphan") and the session inserts the children with the parent, deletes any child removed from the collection (delete-orphan), and cascades deletion from the parent, while the child needs no session or repository of its own - that is how the pattern looks here. The classic hand-written mapper is still the right form when the child must be shared or referenced: then it is a mapped class with its own identity and repository, not a dependent. Django's ORM, by contrast, does not save children with the parent (inline formsets or explicit per-child saves), so it is not a faithful realization of this pattern.
code_sketch:
class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "order"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    lines: Mapped[list["OrderLine"]] = relationship(
        cascade="all, delete-orphan",   # children follow the parent
        passive_deletes=True,            # let the DB's ON DELETE CASCADE work
    )
# session.add(order) writes order + lines; removing a Line marks it deleted.
pitfalls: delete-orphan requires the child to have exactly one parent relationship; pointing another relationship at the same child turns it into an independent entity or raises an error.
passive_deletes=True assumes the database-level ON DELETE CASCADE exists - without it the parent delete leaves orphan rows behind.
Autoflush can insert children earlier than expected when the collection is mutated mid-transaction; keep the mutation and the flush inside one unit of work.
